html:
The Battle of Naseby was fought on 14 June 1645 near the village of Naseby in Northamptonshire, in the middle of England. Parliament's New Model Army beat the main army of King Charles I. It decided the English Civil War.

King and Parliament had been at war since 1642 over who held final power in the state, and over religion. Early in 1645 Parliament formed one national army with regular pay, under Sir Thomas Fairfax, with Oliver Cromwell leading the cavalry. The king had about 9,000 men against about 14,000, but chose to fight. The horsemen of Prince Rupert broke the wing in front of them and then rode on to attack the baggage train. On the other wing Cromwell also won, but he kept most of his men in hand and turned them against the royal infantry in the centre. Surrounded, the foot soldiers surrendered. About 4,500 were taken, with all the king's guns.

The king's private letters were captured too. Parliament printed them, showing that he had sought Irish and foreign troops. He gave himself up in 1646 and was tried and beheaded in 1649. England was a republic for the next eleven years.
